definition: Particle-level properties (rotation, rotation speed, lifetime, speed, direction) are given a range rather than a single fixed value — authored in Roblox's particle editor as a comma-separated min,max pair (e.g. rotation "-360,360") — specifically so that many simultaneously-emitted particles do not all move, spin, or persist identically, which otherwise reads as an obviously synthetic, robotic unison rather than an organic scatter.
purpose: Make a group of particles from one emitter read as many independent, organic instances instead of one repeated, mechanically identical shape.
visible_effect: Particles visibly differ from each other in rotation, spin rate, speed and/or lifespan, rather than all sharing one identical, perfectly synchronized motion.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Uniform, identical particle motion reads as artificial and low-effort; the same particle count with randomized per-instance parameters reads as a richer, more natural effect for very little extra authoring cost.
physical_interpretation: Approximates the real-world fact that many small independent things (embers, dust, sparks) never move in perfect unison, even when they share a common cause.
use_cases: any emitter producing more than one or two particles at a time, where identical per-particle motion would be visible
specifically named in the video for rotation, rotation speed, lifetime and speed, using the min,max comma convention
non_use_cases: a single, isolated particle instance where there is nothing else on screen for it to look identical to
an effect whose whole point is rigid, synchronized repetition (a mechanical readout, a strict grid) where uniformity is the correct read
interactions: concurrent_particle_budget_is_rate_times_lifetime (this same video) — randomizing lifetime specifically also changes the effective concurrent-particle count over time, since not every particle now expires on the same frame
cadence_representation: No direct analogue: VFXSpec's fields (`colorStart`/`colorEnd`, `scale`, `timing`) are declared once per compiled effect, and the per-PARTICLE randomization ranges this video relies on (a rotation or speed range applied independently to each spawned particle) live inside the underlying `primitive` material archetype in `particleLibrary.js`, not as a VFXSpec-level authored field — so a caller cannot widen or narrow a primitive's internal per-particle randomization from `compile_effect` directly.
control_surface: None at the VFXSpec level; whatever randomization ranges exist are baked into the chosen `primitive`'s own implementation.
detection_and_measurement_methods: not measurable in this build — this is a property of the underlying particle system's per-instance value ranges, which Cadence's project data and `ai/motion.js` (built for keyframed rig/item motion) do not represent at all.
generation_or_modification_methods: not applicable — no exposed control surface to modify this per primitive.
failure_modes: leaving rotation, speed, or lifetime at single fixed values for a multi-particle emitter, producing a visibly synthetic, identical-looking swarm
randomizing a property so widely that the effect loses its intended read entirely (not evidenced in this video, but the natural overcorrection of the same technique)
roblox_considerations: Roblox's particle property fields accept a `min,max` pair directly in the same input as a single value (typed as e.g. "-360,360"), which is the specific UI convention this video demonstrates repeatedly across several different properties.
performance_implications: None — randomizing a value range costs nothing extra over a fixed value.
examples: "With stuff like rotation, you can actually just put commas and it'll randomize the value. So, I can go -360 360" (video @ 03:22–03:29)

"it's always nice to mess with the speed of stuff cuz if they're all moving at the same speed, it doesn't look horrible, but it's a very easy way to make it look better if you just randomize the like lifetime and speed a bit" (video @ 32:04–32:16)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/u2o-wHKDlpw @ 03:22–03:29, 32:04–32:16 — Twist demonstrates the comma-range convention on rotation directly and later states the general principle for speed/lifetime explicitly; experimental until validated
